extracted.intended_audience: seminarians, theologians, and students of Catholic dogmatic theology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Catholic dogmatic positions concerning actual and prevenient grace, the gratuity of grace, merit, venial sin, and perseverance as taught by Scripture, Tradition, and Church Councils (notably Orange and Trent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of prevenient and co-operating grace for every salutary act
rubrics_metrics.description: Without prevenient inspiration and the help of the Holy Ghost man cannot believe, hope, love, or be penitent so that justification may be bestowed (cites Second Council of Orange and Council of Trent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported from Scripture (e.g., 'Without me you can do nothing'; St. Paul: 'God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish'), Tradition (St. Augustine, Jerome, Ephraem Syrus), and conciliar definitions. The argument covers beginning, continuation, and completion of salutary acts and is treated as an article of faith; rejects Semipelagianism which ascribes necessary dispositions to natural will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even in sanctifying grace actual graces are necessary for salutary acts (Thesis III)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person in the state of sanctifying grace still requires actual grace (gratia excitans/vocans) to perform salutary acts; sanctifying habits do not obviate the need for actual divine aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as de fide. Justified persons possess supernatural habits but these are not self-moving; concupiscence and weakness remain. Scripture, Tradition (St. Augustine), and the Council of Trent's teaching that Christ 'continually infuses His virtue' are cited. The teaching distinguishes measures of prevenient grace required by justified vs. unjustified persons and stresses continuance of divine assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: All grace is strictly gratuitous; mere nature cannot merit initial grace (Thesis I, gratuity of grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian (initial) grace is a free gift (gratia prima vocans) and cannot be merited de condigno by mere nature; subsequent graces in the order of justification likewise rest on that gratuitous initial grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'merit' and distinguishes condign and congruous merit. Cites Pelagian error, Second Council of Orange, and Council of Trent. Explains that while justified persons can merit de condigno increases and sinners can merit justification de congruo, the initial vocation/grace is absolutely unmerited. The distinction grounds the doctrine of gratuity and resolves apparent tension between merit and gratuitousness by locating all merit in grace's root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and distinctions of merit (condign vs. congruous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit is that property of a good work entitling the performer to a reward; condign merit (meritum de condigno) implies a strict claim measured by commutative justice, whereas congruous merit (meritum de congruo) implies a claim on grounds of fairness or congruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis shows merit requires (1) positively good works, (2) correlation of merit and reward, (3) distinct persons (deserver and rewarder), and (4) basis in justice. Applies these to Creator–creature relation to argue no strict justice relation (so grace is gratuitous). Examples and historical references (Fathers, Scholastics) are given to illustrate distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer and dispositions are distinct from merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayer (humble supplication) and positive/negative dispositions (capacitas s. dispositio) are not equivalent to merit; prayer incites divine mercy, while disposition prepares the subject to receive a form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes purely natural prayer from supernatural prayer. Positive capacity makes a subject apt to receive a new form and may ground expectation, but it differs from quasi-merit; negative capacity is removal of obstacles. Cites doctrinal debate (e.g., Vasquez) and gives examples (angels praying for us without earning merit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Except by a special privilege, man cannot avoid venial sin throughout life (Thesis IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is de fide that, except by a special divine privilege (as for the Blessed Virgin), man in the state of sanctifying grace cannot avoid all venial sins for his entire life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in Councils (Mileve, Trent) and Scripture/Tradition. Clarifies the meaning of 'venial sin', 'in tota vita' (practically limited in time), and 'non posse' (moral, not physical impossibility). Gives theological reasons: concupiscence, imperfect judgement, inconstancy of will, weariness, and God's providential ordering which tolerates sin to guard against pride. Advises faithful to avoid indifference and despondency despite this teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final perseverance requires special divine help and is obtainable by prayer (Thesis V)
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can persevere to the end in righteousness without special help (speciale auxilium) from God; final perseverance is a special gift distinct from sanctifying grace and not automatically merited by good works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Councils (Orange, Trent), Scripture (prayer as means), and St. Augustine's treatise On the Gift of Perseverance. Distinguishes perfect/perseverance types (perfect, imperfect, final; passive vs. active). Emphasizes that prayer—particularly unremitting prayer in the state of grace—can obtain this gift; discusses debates about meritum de congruo vs. prayer as means. Advises perseverance is a 'great gift' requiring efficacious graces and cooperation.
